cards.front: In the mammalian hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, what does the hypothalamus send to the pituitary, in what pattern, and what does the pituitary send to the gonads?
cards.back: GnRH, in pulses. The pituitary answers with LH and FSH, which act on the testes or ovaries.
cards.quote: The hypothalamus sends gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) to the pituitary in pulses, and the pituitary sends luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) to the gonads.

cards.front: In the human ovarian cycle, when does estradiol stop braking the axis and start accelerating it, and what does the switch cause?
cards.back: When estradiol stays high long enough late in the follicular phase. It switches to positive feedback, setting off the LH surge that triggers ovulation.
cards.why: Positive feedback means a signal boosts its own trigger; the timing that matters is how long estradiol stays high.
cards.quote: When estradiol stays high late in the phase, its effect switches to positive feedback, in which a signal boosts its own trigger.

cards.front: In the male hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which two testicular hormones act as brakes, and on what?
cards.back: Testosterone brakes the hypothalamus and pituitary; inhibin B brakes FSH.
cards.quote: testosterone brakes the hypothalamus and pituitary, and inhibin B brakes FSH

cards.front: Castrated male mammals show rising LH and FSH. Testosterone replacement alone restores LH, but FSH stays partly raised. What does this show, and which testicular hormone fits?
cards.back: Testosterone is not the only brake: a second testicular signal restrains FSH. Inhibin B fits, since it brakes FSH.
cards.why: If testosterone alone controlled both gonadotropins, replacing it would have returned FSH to normal too.
cards.quote: In the testis, testosterone brakes the hypothalamus and pituitary, and inhibin B brakes FSH;

cards.front: In the human ovary, which hormone brakes the axis through most of the follicular phase, and which brakes it after ovulation?
cards.back: Estradiol through most of the follicular phase; progesterone after ovulation.
cards.quote: in the ovary, estradiol brakes through most of the follicular phase and progesterone after ovulation.

cards.front: Gametes are {{c1::haploid}} sex cells, cells with one set of chromosomes.
cards.back: Fertilization joins two gametes into a diploid zygote with two sets.
cards.quote: Gametes are haploid sex cells, cells with one set of chromosomes.

cards.front: Where in the human testis does spermatogenesis take place?
cards.back: In the seminiferous tubules, coiled tubes inside each testis. Germ cells mature as they move from the tubule wall toward its centre.
cards.quote: Spermatogenesis happens in the seminiferous tubules, coiled tubes inside each testis.

cards.front: What do human spermatogonia do at the wall of the seminiferous tubule?
cards.back: They divide by mitosis, renewing themselves through adult life and feeding cells into meiosis. They are diploid (46 chromosomes).
cards.quote: divide by mitosis at the wall, renewing themselves through adult life and feeding cells into meiosis

cards.front: Trace chromosome number and chromatids from one human primary spermatocyte to the sperm.
cards.back: Primary spermatocyte (46) → meiosis I separates paired chromosomes → 2 secondary spermatocytes (23, each of two chromatids) → meiosis II separates chromatids → 4 spermatids (23 single) → spermiogenesis → sperm.
cards.quote: Meiosis II separates the chromatids, giving four spermatids, each with 23 single chromosomes.

cards.front: In the human testis, which cells line the seminiferous tubules and support developing sperm cells, and which cells between the tubules supply the hormone that helps them?
cards.back: Sertoli cells line the tubules; Leydig cells between the tubules make testosterone.
cards.quote: Sertoli support relies on testosterone's help

cards.front: After leaving the human testis, where do sperm mature, which duct carries them onward, and which glands add fluid to make semen?
cards.back: They mature in the epididymis, pass through the vas deferens, and the seminal vesicles and prostate add fluid.
cards.quote: Sperm then mature in the epididymis, a coiled duct on the testis.

cards.front: In human females, when are primary oocytes formed, and at what stage do they arrest?
cards.back: Before birth, in the fetal ovary. They enter meiosis I and arrest in prophase I, each waiting in a follicle for years or decades.
cards.quote: which enter meiosis I and arrest in prophase I

cards.front: In humans, what triggers the oocyte to finish meiosis I, at what stage is the secondary oocyte released, and when does it finish meiosis II?
cards.back: The LH surge, shortly before ovulation. It is released arrested in metaphase II and finishes meiosis II only if fertilized, giving the egg proper and a second polar body.
cards.quote: It finishes meiosis II only if fertilized, giving the egg proper and a second polar body.

cards.front: What is unequal about meiosis I in a human oocyte, and what is a polar body?
cards.back: Nearly all the cytoplasm goes to the secondary oocyte. The other chromosome set leaves in a small cell, the polar body.
cards.quote: The division is unequal: nearly all the cytoplasm goes to the secondary oocyte, and the other chromosome set leaves in a small polar body.

cards.front: Contrast the human testis and ovary in gamete supply and in gametes per meiosis.
cards.back: The testis renews its stock (spermatogonia) and makes four gametes per meiosis. The ovary spends a stock laid down before birth and makes one gamete per meiosis.
cards.quote: The testis renews its stock and makes four gametes per meiosis; the ovary spends a stock laid down before birth, one gamete per meiosis.

cards.front: Suppose 35 human primary spermatocytes complete both meiotic divisions and a hypothetical 60 percent of the spermatids survive to become sperm. How many spermatids form, how many sperm result, and how many are lost?
cards.back: 35 x 4 = 140 spermatids; 140 x 0.60 = 84 sperm; 140 - 84 = 56 lost.
cards.why: Each primary spermatocyte gives four spermatids after meiosis I and II.
cards.quote: Each gives 4 spermatids: 120 x 4 = 480 spermatids.

cards.front: Suppose 45 human primary oocytes each completed both meiotic divisions (an idealization). How many eggs result, and about how many polar bodies?
cards.back: 45 eggs, one per oocyte. Polar bodies: 2 or 3 per oocyte, so 90 to 135 in all.
cards.why: The first polar body may or may not divide again; in reality meiosis II finishes only on fertilization.
cards.quote: The other chromosome sets leave in the polar bodies, two or three per oocyte (the first polar body may or may not divide again).

cards.front: Two 40-year-old people: one ovulates an oocyte, the other ejaculates sperm. Reasoning from how each gamete line is supplied, compare the oocyte arrested for years or decades with how long sperm production takes.
cards.back: The oocyte entered meiosis I before birth and sat arrested in prophase I for years or decades. Sperm come from spermatogonia renewed through adult life; spermatogenesis takes roughly 64 to 74 days.
cards.why: Rests on the ovary spending a stock laid down before birth and the testis renewing its stock.
cards.quote: Each waits, for years or decades, in a follicle, the oocyte plus the supporting cells around it.

cards.front: Why does a steady supply of GnRH fail to keep LH and FSH up, according to the usual explanation?
cards.back: Desensitization: under constant GnRH, the pituitary cells that make LH and FSH turn their response down.
cards.why: The monkey experiment itself did not identify the mechanism.
cards.quote: The usual answer is desensitization: under constant GnRH, the pituitary cells that make LH and FSH turn their response down.

cards.front: Rhesus monkeys with hypothalamic lesions got GnRH either as hourly pulses or as a steady drip at one of four rates. Only pulses restored LH. Why does the dose comparison matter?
cards.back: At the two highest drip rates, the drip delivered as much GnRH as the pulses or more, so too little hormone cannot explain the failure. The time pattern carries the message.
cards.quote: at the two highest it delivered as much GnRH as the pulses or more, so too little hormone cannot explain the failure.

cards.front: In the continuous-versus-pulsed GnRH experiment, why can simple saturation of the pituitary response not explain the drip's failure?
cards.back: A saturated response would plateau, not fall below the pulsed response at the same or higher dose. The drip's response fell below it, so saturation alone is ruled out.
cards.quote: A response that merely saturated would not fall below the pulsed response at the same or a higher dose, so saturation alone is ruled out.

cards.front: A hypothetical long-acting drug keeps pituitary GnRH receptors stimulated continuously in an adult man. Predict what happens over weeks to LH, FSH, testosterone and spermatogenesis, and why.
cards.back: By the rule, LH and FSH output would fall, so testosterone and spermatogenesis would lose support. Rule: sustained GnRH desensitizes the gonadotrophs, which turn their response down.
cards.quote: In desensitization, sustained GnRH triggers adaptive changes in the gonadotrophs (the pituitary cells that make LH and FSH)

cards.front: In mice, brief light-driven activation of kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus evoked LH pulses, and silencing them suppressed the pulses. What does this show?
cards.back: In mice, kisspeptin neurons in the hypothalamus drive the pulses. In primates the pulse source is unsettled.
cards.quote: brief light-driven activation of those neurons evoked LH pulses, and silencing them suppressed the pulses.

cards.front: Through which receptor types do the gonadotropins (LH, FSH) and the ovarian steroids (estradiol, progesterone) mainly act?
cards.back: LH and FSH: G-protein-coupled receptors. Estradiol and progesterone: receptors inside the cell (nuclear receptors).
cards.quote: Estradiol and progesterone act mainly through receptors inside the cell (nuclear receptors).

cards.front: In the human follicular phase, how do theca and granulosa cells divide the work of making estradiol?
cards.back: LH drives theca cells to make androgens; FSH-supported granulosa cells convert those androgens to estradiol.
cards.quote: LH drives theca cells to make androgens, and FSH-supported granulosa cells convert them to estradiol.

cards.front: In a growing human follicle, the granulosa cells lose their FSH support while theca cells still get LH. Predict the effect on estradiol and on endometrial rebuilding.
cards.back: Estradiol falls: theca androgens are not converted. With less estradiol, the proliferative rebuilding of the endometrium would be weaker.
cards.why: Two-cell rule: LH drives theca androgens; FSH-supported granulosa cells convert them to estradiol, which rebuilds the lining.
cards.quote: FSH-supported granulosa cells convert them to estradiol

cards.front: What two events does the LH surge set off in the human ovary?
cards.back: The oocyte finishes meiosis I, and ovulation releases the secondary oocyte.
cards.quote: LH release rises steeply in the LH surge, which sets the oocyte finishing meiosis I and triggers ovulation

cards.front: In the human luteal phase, what does the emptied follicle become, what does it secrete, and what does progesterone do?
cards.back: The corpus luteum, secreting progesterone and estradiol. Progesterone converts the endometrium into a receptive secretory lining and brakes LH and FSH.
cards.quote: After ovulation, in the luteal phase, the emptied follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone and estradiol.

cards.front: In a human cycle with no implantation, what chain of events leads to menstruation?
cards.back: The corpus luteum regresses, progesterone falls, and the lining breaks down in menstruation, beginning the next cycle.
cards.quote: If no embryo implants, the corpus luteum regresses, progesterone falls, and the lining breaks down in menstruation, which begins the next cycle.

cards.front: Match the human ovarian phases to the uterine phases.
cards.back: Follicular phase = menstruation plus the proliferative phase. Luteal phase = secretory phase.
cards.quote: the follicular phase spans menstruation and the proliferative phase, and the luteal phase is the secretory phase.

cards.front: A woman's cycles are regularly 32 days long and her luteal phase lasts about 12 days. On about which day did she ovulate, and how long was her follicular phase?
cards.back: 32 - 12 = 20: ovulation around day 20; follicular phase about 20 days.
cards.why: Cycle = follicular + luteal phase; day-14 ovulation belongs to the 28-day drawing convention.
cards.quote: The textbook 28-day cycle with day-14 ovulation is a drawing convention

cards.front: Early in a human pregnancy, a hypothetical drug blocks progesterone receptors. Predict the effect on the uterine lining, and why.
cards.back: By the lesson's rule, the lining would likely break down, as if progesterone had fallen, endangering the pregnancy. Progesterone holds the receptive secretory lining; blocking its action mimics progesterone falling.
cards.quote: Progesterone converts the thickened endometrium into a lining that can receive an embryo, the secretory phase, and it brakes LH and FSH again.

cards.front: In early human pregnancy, what makes hCG, through which receptor does it act, and what does it do?
cards.back: The embryo's trophoblast. Acting through the LH receptor, hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone, so the lining is not shed.
cards.quote: Acting through the LH receptor, hCG keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone, so the lining is not shed.

cards.front: The corpus luteum is lost at week 6 in one human pregnancy and at week 11 in another. Which pregnancy loses its main progesterone source, and why?
cards.back: The week-6 pregnancy. Before about weeks 7 to 9 the corpus luteum, kept by hCG, is the main source; by week 11 the placenta has taken over.
cards.quote: From about weeks 7 to 9 of gestation, the placenta itself becomes the main source of progesterone.

cards.front: In a hypothetical cycle, the dominant follicle's estradiol rises but never stays high for long. Predict ovulation and the luteal phase, and name the rule.
cards.back: No switch to positive feedback, so no LH surge and no ovulation; no corpus luteum forms, so no luteal progesterone and no secretory phase. Rule: sustained high estradiol is what sets off the surge.
cards.quote: Here the timing that matters is how long estradiol stays high, a different signal from the GnRH pulses in the monkeys.

cards.front: Name four forms of asexual reproduction in animals, with an example animal for the first three.
cards.back: Budding (Hydra); fission (some sea anemones and flatworms); fragmentation (some sea stars); parthenogenesis (an egg develops without fertilization).
cards.quote: In budding a new individual grows out of the parent, as in Hydra

cards.front: What is the twofold cost of males?
cards.back: If every female leaves two young, an asexual female's are both daughters that will bear young; a sexual female's are on average a daughter and a son, and the son bears none.
cards.why: So asexual females double each generation while sexual females stay level, all else equal.
cards.quote: a sexual female's are on average one daughter and one son, and the son bears no young himself.

cards.front: In a made-up population, one asexual and one sexual female each leave two surviving young per generation. Counting only females, what share of females is asexual after five generations?
cards.back: Asexual: 2^5 = 32; sexual stays at 1. Share = 32/33, about 97 percent.
cards.quote: asexual females go 1, 2, 4, 8 over three generations, while each sexual female leaves one daughter, so sexual females stay at 1.

cards.front: Besides the twofold cost, what other cost does sex usually carry, and what does it offer?
cards.back: Finding a mate. It offers new combinations of alleles. Why sex persists despite its costs is still argued.
cards.quote: Sex usually also means finding a mate, a cost asexual reproduction avoids; it offers new combinations of alleles.

cards.front: Water fleas (Daphnia) and many aphids make generations of females by parthenogenesis, then males and sexual eggs, often as the season turns. Reasoning from the costs and benefits of sex, what might each phase gain?
cards.back: Parthenogenetic phases avoid the twofold cost and mate-finding, so numbers grow fast; the sexual phase offers new allele combinations. Rests on the lesson's cost-benefit rules; why sex persists is still argued.
cards.quote: water fleas (Daphnia) and many aphids make generations of females by parthenogenesis, then males and sexual eggs, often as the season turns.

cards.front: In which direction do clownfish and many wrasses change sex?
cards.back: Clownfish start as males and the largest can become female; many wrasses change from female to male.
cards.quote: clownfish start as males and the largest can become female, while many wrasses change from female to male.

cards.front: What advantages does internal fertilization give over external fertilization?
cards.back: Sperm arrive close to the eggs, and on land the gametes are kept from drying out.
cards.quote: Sperm arrive close to the eggs, and on land the gametes are kept from drying out.

cards.front: A broadcast-spawning sea urchin and a bird each release the same number of eggs. Whose eggs are more likely to go unfertilized, and why?
cards.back: The sea urchin's. Released into the sea, many gametes never meet; the bird fertilizes internally, so sperm arrive close to the eggs.
cards.quote: Sea urchins broadcast-spawn, releasing eggs and sperm into the sea, where many gametes never meet and eggs and larvae are exposed to predators.

cards.front: How do the estrous cycles of most mammals differ from menstrual cycles?
cards.back: The endometrium is generally reabsorbed rather than shed, and females are usually receptive mainly around ovulation.
cards.quote: Most mammals have estrous cycles instead of menstrual cycles: the endometrium is generally reabsorbed rather than shed, and females are usually receptive mainly around ovulation.

cards.front: In the parthenogenetic lizard Aspidoscelis neomexicana, FISH showed that sister chromosomes, not homologues, pair in meiosis. How does this let all-female lizards keep meiosis yet pass on the mother's heterozygosity?
cards.back: Crossing over between identical sister copies changes nothing, and the two divisions return the doubled set to diploid. The egg keeps both of the mother's different versions of each chromosome.
cards.why: Shown only for chromosomes the probes could tell apart, in these Aspidoscelis species.
cards.quote: the partners paired in meiosis were sister chromosomes (copies of the same chromosome), not the two different homologues (the maternal and paternal versions) a sexual animal pairs.

cards.front: Oocyte chromosomes of parthenogenetic Aspidoscelis tesselata had about 2.2 times the DAPI volume of sexual A. gularis, but body-cell DNA differed by less than 1 percent. What does the body-cell result rule out?
cards.back: A simply bigger genome. The doubling belongs to the germ line, before meiosis.
cards.quote: In body cells (nucleated red blood cells), DNA content differed by less than 1 percent.
